paragraphs.paraphrase: While Odysseus sleeps, Athena goes to the city of the Phaeacians, who used to live in Hypereia near the lawless Cyclopes until the stronger Cyclopes raided them and their king Nausithous moved them to remote Scheria, where he walled the city, built houses and temples and shared out the land. Nausithous has since died, and King Alcinous, whose wisdom comes from the gods, now rules. Athena heads to his palace to help get Odysseus home.

barriers.quote: near the lawless Cyclopes
barriers.my_reading: A lawless, stronger neighbouring people who raided the Phaeacians; the text never says what the Cyclopes are.
barriers.note: outside knowledge only; the plural name is also awkward aloud

barriers.quote: But he was dead and gone to the house of Hades
barriers.my_reading: Nausithous has died ('the house of Hades' = the land of the dead) and Alcinous now rules; whether Alcinous is his son is not stated.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Athena goes into the richly decorated bedroom of Nausicaa, King Alcinous's beautiful daughter, where two pretty maids sleep on either side of the closed double doors. Disguised as the daughter of Dymas, a famous sea captain, who is Nausicaa's close friend and the same age, Athena drifts to the bedside like a breath of air, hovers over her head and speaks.

barriers.quote: the famous sea captain Dymas’s daughter
barriers.my_reading: Dymas is the famous sea captain; Athena takes the shape of his daughter, Nausicaa's friend.
barriers.note: stacked possessive; aloud it is unclear whether the captain or the daughter is famous, or whom Athena imitates

barriers.quote: coming up to the girl’s bedside like a breath of wind, she hovered over her head
barriers.my_reading: Athena appears to Nausicaa in a dream, slipping in past the closed doors like air; that it is a dream is only revealed in paragraph 4.

paragraphs.paraphrase: In the friend's guise, Athena scolds Nausicaa for being lazy: her clothes are lying around in a mess though she will marry soon and must be well dressed and supply good clothes for her attendants, which earns a good name and makes her parents proud. She proposes a washing day at dawn tomorrow and offers to help, since all the best young Phaeacian men are courting Nausicaa and she will soon be married. Nausicaa should ask her father for a mule wagon to carry the rugs, robes and belts, and ride rather than walk, as the washing places are far from town.

barriers.quote: you are going to be married almost immediately
barriers.my_reading: She is not engaged; the point is that suitors are courting her and she will marry soon, so she should get her clothes ready.
barriers.note: first reads as if a wedding were already arranged

barriers.quote: should find good clothes for those who attend you
barriers.my_reading: Her attendants (perhaps the wedding party, perhaps her maids) will need good clothes too.

barriers.quote: the washing cisterns
barriers.my_reading: stone washing pools or tanks by the river
barriers.note: 'cisterns' suggests underground water tanks; later also called 'pits' (paragraph 8)

paragraphs.paraphrase: Athena then returns to Olympus, said to be the gods' everlasting home, where there is no rough wind, rain or snow, only endless sunshine and calm light in which the happy gods live forever.

In the morning Nausicaa wakes, puzzling over her dream, and goes to tell her parents. Her mother is by the fire with her maids, spinning purple yarn, and Nausicaa catches her father as he is leaving for a council meeting called by the Phaeacian leaders, and stops him.

barriers.quote: to tell her father and mother all about it
barriers.my_reading: She meant to tell them about the dream, but in the event she only asks for the wagon and says nothing about marriage (paragraph 6).

paragraphs.paraphrase: Nausicaa sweetly asks her father for a big wagon to take the family's dirty clothes to the river. She says he, as the chief man, should wear a clean shirt to council, and her five brothers (two married, three handsome bachelors) always want clean clothes for dances.

She is too shy to mention her own marriage, but her father understands. He grants her the mules and anything else she wants, and says the servants will get her a sturdy wagon with a box big enough for all the clothes.

barriers.quote: a good strong wagon with a body to it
barriers.my_reading: a wagon with a box or bed on it to carry the load
barriers.note: 'with a body to it' sounds odd

paragraphs.paraphrase: The servants bring out the wagon and harness the mules while Nausicaa loads the clothes; her mother packs a basket of food and a skin of wine, and gives her a golden flask of oil for her and her maids to rub on their skin. Nausicaa takes the whip and reins and drives off, and the mules trot steadily, carrying her, the laundry and her maids.

barriers.quote: so that she and her women could anoint themselves
barriers.my_reading: rub oil on their skin after bathing, like a body lotion
barriers.note: 'anoint' sounds religious; the custom recurs in paragraphs 8, 16 and 17 unexplained

paragraphs.paraphrase: At the river's washing pools, which always have plenty of clean running water, they let the mules graze, then compete at trampling the clothes clean in the pits and spread them to dry on the pebbly beach. They bathe, oil themselves, eat beside the stream, then take off their head veils and play ball while Nausicaa sings. Just as Artemis the huntress, hunting on the mountains with her nymphs, stands a head taller than all of them, to her mother Leto's pride, so Nausicaa outshines her maids.

barriers.quote: vied with one another in treading them in the pits
barriers.my_reading: They competed at trampling the clothes with their feet in the washing pools to get the dirt out.
barriers.note: washing by treading is unfamiliar; 'pits' = the 'cisterns' of paragraph 2

barriers.quote: a high beach of shingle
barriers.my_reading: a beach of pebbles
barriers.note: British usage; many readers think of roof shingles

barriers.quote: Then they had their dinner
barriers.my_reading: their midday meal; it is still daytime and the clothes are drying
barriers.note: 'dinner' suggests evening, which muddles the timeline

barriers.quote: daughters of aegis-bearing Zeus
barriers.my_reading: 'aegis-bearing' is a title of Zeus (he carries something called the aegis); the text never explains it.
barriers.note: outside knowledge only; recurs in paragraph 24

barriers.quote: Leto is proud then to see her daughter
barriers.my_reading: Leto is Artemis's mother, inferable only from 'her daughter'.
barriers.note: long run-on simile; hard to follow aloud

paragraphs.paraphrase: As they fold the clothes into the wagon to go home, Athena plans for Odysseus to wake and meet the girl who will guide him to the Phaeacians' city. So when Nausicaa throws a ball at a maid, it misses and lands in deep water, everyone shrieks, and the noise wakes Odysseus, who sits up in his bed of leaves wondering what is happening.

Odysseus wonders what kind of people he has come among: savage and lawless, or hospitable and decent? He hears young women's voices that sound like nymphs of mountains, springs and meadows, concludes that at any rate there are human beings here, and decides to go and look.

barriers.quote: At any rate I am among a race of men and women
barriers.my_reading: Whether or not they are nymphs, he is at least among human beings who can talk (not monsters or wild creatures).
barriers.note: the jump from 'nymphs' to 'men and women' is abrupt

paragraphs.paraphrase: He crawls out of the bushes holding a leafy branch over his genitals and, naked, filthy and driven by need, approaches the girls looking like a hungry mountain lion that braves wind and rain to raid a fenced farmyard. The maids scatter along the sandbars, but Nausicaa, given courage by Athena, stands her ground and faces him. Odysseus debates whether to clasp her knees as a suppliant or plead from where he stands for clothes and directions, and chooses to keep his distance so as not to offend her, speaking in flattering, persuasive words.

barriers.quote: Even such did Odysseus seem to the young women
barriers.my_reading: To the girls he looked as frightening and desperate as the hungry lion; 'for he was in great want' means need drove him to approach them naked.
barriers.note: archaic 'Even such' and 'in great want'; the simile also slips into the present tense

barriers.quote: scampered off along the spits that jutted out into the sea
barriers.my_reading: ran off along narrow points of sand or land sticking out into the sea
barriers.note: 'spits'

barriers.quote: embrace her knees as a suppliant
barriers.my_reading: Kneeling and hugging someone's knees was the formal way to beg for protection; the custom is not explained, so the reader must infer why he would do it and why a naked stranger clasping a girl's knees might offend.
barriers.note: outside knowledge only for the custom's force

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus calls Nausicaa 'queen', begs her help and asks if she is a goddess (surely Artemis) or a mortal; if mortal, her parents and siblings must be proud of her, and happiest will be the man who wins her with the richest gifts and takes her home. He has never seen such beauty, except a young palm tree he once admired beside Apollo's altar at Delos, on the journey with many followers that began his troubles. He dares not clasp her knees but is desperate: yesterday was his twentieth day at sea since leaving the Ogygian island, and he expects fate still has more suffering in store.

barriers.quote: O queen
barriers.my_reading: A flattering form of address; she is an unmarried princess and he does not yet know who she is.
barriers.note: can suggest he takes her for the queen

barriers.quote: the man whose wedding gifts have been the richest
barriers.my_reading: The suitor who offers the most gifts (to her family) wins her as a bride; modern readers think of wedding presents from guests.
barriers.note: outside knowledge only (bride-gift custom)

barriers.quote: on the journey that has been the source of all my troubles
barriers.my_reading: Some earlier voyage with a large following, probably the expedition to Troy, but the text does not say.
barriers.note: outside knowledge only

barriers.quote: the Ogygian island
barriers.my_reading: Calypso's island, which Book 5 never named; inferable only from the twenty days at sea.

paragraphs.paraphrase: He asks her to pity him, as she is the first person he has met here, to show him the way to town, and to give him any cloth she used to wrap the laundry so he can cover himself. He wishes her all she desires (a husband, a home and harmony), since nothing is better than a husband and wife of one mind: it galls their enemies, pleases their friends, and they themselves feel it most.

barriers.quote: let me have anything you may have brought here to wrap your clothes in
barriers.my_reading: He is naked and wants any spare cloth, even a laundry wrapper, to cover himself; the purpose is left implicit.

barriers.quote: and they themselves know more about it than anyone
barriers.my_reading: The couple themselves know best how good it is (or: they get the best reputation); the ending is vague.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Nausicaa replies that he seems sensible and decent, but luck cannot be explained: Zeus gives good fortune to rich and poor as he chooses, so Odysseus must bear what he has been sent. Now that he is here, he will lack neither clothes nor anything else a needy stranger may reasonably expect. She will show him the way to town, and tells him her people are the Phaeacians and she is the daughter of Alcinous, who holds all power in the land.

barriers.quote: you appear to be a sensible, well-disposed person. There is no accounting for luck.
barriers.my_reading: The link is implied: he seems a good man, so his misfortune does not mean he deserves it; luck is simply Zeus's choice.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Nausicaa calls her fleeing maids back: he is no robber or murderer, and nobody can harm the Phaeacians, who are loved by the gods and live apart on a remote headland in the loud sea with no dealings with anyone else. This is a poor lost man and they must be kind, because Zeus protects strangers in need, who are grateful for whatever they get. She tells them to give him food and drink and bathe him in the stream in a sheltered spot.

barriers.quote: a land’s end that juts into the sounding sea
barriers.my_reading: a remote point of land sticking out into the loud, roaring sea
barriers.note: 'sounding' = loud, not measuring depth

barriers.quote: They will take what they can get and be thankful
barriers.my_reading: Even a small gift is welcome to such people (so be kind), though it can read as dismissive.

paragraphs.paraphrase: The maids return, seat Odysseus in a sheltered spot, give him a tunic and cloak and the golden flask of oil, and tell him to wash in the stream. He asks them to stand aside so he can wash off the salt and oil his skin, which he has not done in a long time, because he is embarrassed to strip in front of pretty young women.

The maids step away and tell Nausicaa while Odysseus scrubs the salt off his body and hair, oils himself and puts on the clothes. Athena makes him look taller and stronger and gives him thick curling hair like hyacinth flowers, adding beauty to his head and shoulders as a master craftsman overlays silver with gold. He sits apart on the beach looking young and handsome, and Nausicaa gazes at him admiringly and speaks to her maids.

barriers.quote: flow down in curls like hyacinth blossoms
barriers.my_reading: thick, tightly curling hair like the clustered petals of hyacinths (perhaps dark in colour)
barriers.note: hard to picture

barriers.quote: as a skillful workman enriches a piece of silver plate by gilding it
barriers.my_reading: Athena adds beauty to him as a craftsman overlays silver with gold; the aside about Hephaestus (unexplained, apparently a god of craft) interrupts the sentence.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Nausicaa tells her maids she believes the gods sent this man to the Phaeacians: at first he looked ordinary, now he looks like a god. She would like a husband like him, if only he would stay; meanwhile they should give him food and drink.

barriers.quote: I should like my future husband to be just such a man as he is, if only he would stay here
barriers.my_reading: She is hinting that she would like him himself as her husband if he stayed, not just someone like him.

paragraphs.paraphrase: The maids feed Odysseus, who eats and drinks ravenously after his long fast. Meanwhile Nausicaa, turning to something else, has the laundry folded and loaded, yokes the mules, takes her seat and calls to Odysseus.

barriers.quote: Meanwhile Nausicaa thought of another matter
barriers.my_reading: She turns her mind to getting back to town (and perhaps how to bring the stranger without scandal); vague.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Nausicaa tells Odysseus to come back to town; she will introduce him at her father's house, where he will meet the leading Phaeacians, but he must do as she says. While they pass the farmland he should walk briskly behind the wagon with the maids, and soon they will reach the town: walled all round, with a harbour on each side and a narrow way in, ships pulled up along the road, each in its owner's place, and a paved marketplace around a temple of Poseidon. There people trade ship's gear and make oars, because the Phaeacians are not archers but seafarers who take pride in their ships.

barriers.quote: I will introduce you at the house of my excellent father
barriers.my_reading: She will see that he is received there, although in paragraph 22 it turns out he must arrive separately and present himself to her mother.

barriers.quote: a good harbor on either side with a narrow entrance into the city
barriers.my_reading: The town sits on a strip of land with a harbour on each side, reached by a narrow way in; hard to picture.

barriers.quote: the ships drawn up along the roadside
barriers.my_reading: ships hauled out of the water and parked beside the road

barriers.quote: with a temple of Poseidon in the middle of it, paved with large stones bedded in the earth
barriers.my_reading: The marketplace (probably not the temple) is paved with large stones set into the ground.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Nausicaa explains she fears gossip from spiteful townspeople: some lowlife might say, who is this handsome stranger with Nausicaa, is she going to marry some drifting foreign sailor (since they have no neighbours), or a god sent in answer to her prayers? Let her go and find a husband elsewhere, since she snubs all the fine local men who love her. She says she could not blame them, as she herself would disapprove of any girl who went about with men against public opinion, while her parents were alive and before a proper public wedding.

barriers.quote: for we have no neighbors
barriers.my_reading: He cannot have come from a nearby people, so he must have come off a foreign ship.

barriers.quote: It would be a good thing if she would take herself off and find a husband somewhere else
barriers.my_reading: The gossip sneers that she is too proud for local men and might as well go off and find a foreign husband; unclear whether it is a wish or a sarcastic comment.
barriers.note: nested quotation inside her speech; hard to follow aloud

barriers.quote: while her father and mother were still alive
barriers.my_reading: Probably: a girl whose parents are alive should let them arrange things rather than choose men herself; the reason is not stated.

barriers.quote: without having been married in the face of all the world
barriers.my_reading: before being publicly married
barriers.note: archaic

paragraphs.paraphrase: If Odysseus wants her father to send him home, he must follow her plan: wait in a roadside poplar grove sacred to Athena, near her father's estate within shouting distance of town, until she has reached the palace, then walk into town and ask for Alcinous's house, which any child can point out as the finest. Once through the gates and courtyards, he should go straight to her mother, who will be spinning purple wool by the fire, leaning against a pillar with her maids behind her, next to the seat where her father sits drinking like a god. He should ignore the king and clasp the queen's knees, and if he wins her over, he can hope to get home however far away it is.

barriers.quote: give you an escort
barriers.my_reading: passage home by ship with a crew (as Zeus predicted in Book 5), not a bodyguard

barriers.quote: one of the bearing-posts
barriers.my_reading: a load-bearing pillar holding up the roof

barriers.quote: Never mind him, but go up to my mother, and lay your hands on her knees
barriers.my_reading: He should appeal to the queen as a formal suppliant; why the queen rather than Alcinous, who holds 'the whole power of the state' (paragraph 14), is not explained.
barriers.note: knee-clasping custom again unexplained

paragraphs.paraphrase: Nausicaa whips up the mules and they leave the river, driving carefully so that Odysseus and the maids, walking behind, can keep up. At sunset they reach Athena's sacred grove, where Odysseus sits down and prays to Athena, the daughter of Zeus.

Odysseus prays to Athena, the tireless daughter of Zeus, to hear him now, since she ignored his prayers while Poseidon was wrecking him. He asks her to pity him and let the Phaeacians receive him kindly as a friend.

barriers.quote: daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus, unwearying
barriers.my_reading: 'unwearying' describes Athena (tireless), not Zeus; it dangles at the end of the phrase.
barriers.note: 'aegis-bearing' again unexplained

barriers.quote: for you paid no heed to my prayers when Poseidon was wrecking me
barriers.my_reading: From Odysseus's point of view she did not answer him during the storm, though Book 5 showed her helping him (calming the winds, guiding him, sending sleep); the 'for' logic (hear me now because you did not then) is also odd.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Athena hears his prayer but does not appear to him openly, because she is wary of her uncle Poseidon, who is still furiously trying to stop Odysseus from getting home.

barriers.quote: she was afraid of her uncle Poseidon
barriers.my_reading: Poseidon is Zeus's brother and so Athena's uncle; she avoids defying him openly. Why he is so set against Odysseus is still not explained.

book_level: Supplication (embracing someone's knees as a formal plea) is the key move of the Book (paragraphs 11, 12, 22) but is never explained: why it is the proper way to beg, why it might offend, and why Odysseus must do it to the queen rather than the king who holds all power (14 vs 22).

Nausicaa's instructions (20-22) are the hardest stretch: a town layout that is hard to picture, an imagined gossip speech nested inside her speech (hard to follow aloud), and a social argument ('while her father and mother were still alive', 'take herself off') whose logic is unclear; she also says she will introduce him, then sends him in alone.

Customs are assumed rather than explained: oiling the skin after bathing ('anoint', 7, 8, 16, 17), washing clothes by treading them in pits, bride gifts deciding who marries (12), a goddess visiting in disguise in a dream (only revealed as a dream in paragraph 4).
Unexplained references: Cyclopes, aegis-bearing Zeus, Leto, Hephaestus, the Delos journey, and 'the Ogygian island' (Calypso's island was never named in Book 5).
Odysseus's complaint that Athena ignored his prayers (24) clashes with Book 5, where she helped him repeatedly; paragraph 25 only partly explains it. Poseidon's motive is still never given.

Mostly readable modern prose, but old-fashioned forms remain: 'O queen' for a princess, 'Even such', 'in great want', 'shingle', 'spits', 'bearing-posts', 'sounding sea', 'in the face of all the world'.
